The Reverend Francis Borland wrote a History of this event, which stated that a conflict arose between the "Minifters" and the "Counfellors" over the building of Fort Saint Andrew. One leader hightailed with his posse out of the central location of this event on the vessels Speedy Return and Continent, after that group was attacked by Spanish mercenaries and privateers at Madeira, and the main action of this event never occurred because of a mosquito infestation in the jungles. Immediately after this event, the Norwich Post had the tabloid "The Damned Fiasco" as a result of the Thomas Drummond's failure to set up a fishery in the Bay of Caledonia. This event led to the Act of Union of 1707 resulting in one nation going bankrupt. For 10 points identify this event in which Scotland attempted to establish a colonial holding in Panama.

This royal family employed the diplomat Count von Trauttmansdorff, who represented their interests during the Thirty Years War. The Zrinski-Frankopan Conspiracy was one attempt to overthrow this royal family. One ruler from this family was nicknamed "the king with a hat" for his refusal to take part in a coronation ceremony. Forces loyal to this family won the Battle of Slankamen. Following the death of the last Medici, a female member of this royal family became Grand Duchess of Tuscany, and thereby the ruler of Florence. In the 19th century, this family took the title "King of Lombardy-Venetia". At the Treaty of Prague, this family gave up the title of President of the German Confederation. That came after the nation this family ruled was defeated at the Battle of Koniggratz by Prussia. Name this royal family of Austria.

Richard von Glahn argued that traditional historiography of this man ignores his role in reshaping his country's foreign policy. This man captured King Vira Alakeshwara during a war he fought against the Kingdom of Kotte, after which this man placed a trilingual inscription at Galle that boasted of the treasure he donated to a local temple. This man most likely took advantage of the Kangnido Map. This man is known to have traded gold and silver in exchange for camels and a giraffe at Malindi. A document from Malacca which suggests he was a member of the Hanafi Sect is the basis for the oft-made claim that he was a Muslim. This man's deeds were banned under the isolation policies of the Hongxi Emperor. Name this Chinese explorer from the Ming Dynasty.

In one position, this man worked with Ephraim Williams in an expedition where Seth Pomeroy lost most of his contingent in the Crown Point Campaign. While in that same position, he published a work which stated "What does the creditor have a right to demand a debt to be contracted, or for the debtor to oblige that payment?" and explains the role of "Bills of Credit." This author of A Caveat Against Injustice obtained his highest position when William Johnson resigned from his position in the Senate. At one meeting, this member of the Committee of Five put forth an idea which was modified in the Committee of Detail; that plan opposed other ideas proposed by William Paterson, and James Madison. He represented a state at the Constitutional Convention with Oliver Ellsworth. Name this politician whose Great Compromise was adopted by the legislative branch giving each of the states proportional representation, a founding father from Connecticut.

A political cartoon from Punch depicts this Frenchman watching as a kneeling German statesman claims he is drowning,telling him to "try standing up on your feet." This politician served as president of the review committee and the drivingforce behind France's 1905 state secularism law. With Jean Jaures, this man founded the eventually communist publicationL'Humanite, and later succeeded Georges Clemenceau as prime minister after the latter's fiÂrst term. This statesman attendedthe Washington Naval Conference in 1921, and four years later produced a set of agreements that guaranteed the borders ofWestern Europe while leaving the German-Polish border undetermined. Those treaties were negotiated with Gustav Stresemannand Austen Chamberlain. He's best known for a 1928 treaty in which he convinced a large number of countries tooutlaw war. Name this Nobel Peace Laureate who negotiated the Locarno Treaties and a pact named for himand Frank Kellogg.

A missionary from this country reportedly claimed land for his monarch in front of 14 gathered tribes while singing "VexillaRegis" and "Te Deum." A geographer from this country led a group sent to Ecuador to measure the Earth at its equator, andmade the Âfirst European map of the Amazon basin. The fiÂnal voyage of an explorer from this country ended in humiliationwhen his men brought back a load of minerals they thought were diamond and gold, but turned out to be iron pyrite andquartz. This country established the Company of One Hundred Associates to control its holdings, after one of its explorersdiscovered the villages of Stadacona and Hochelaga. While sailing under this country's flflag, the coast of Rhode Island was exploredby Verrazano. A man from this nation founded Anticosti Island and Prince Edward Island, before exploring the SaintLawrence River. Name this European country that sent men like Jacques Cartier to the New World.

Under Roman rule, this city was home to a set of public baths where coins featuring both Gordian III and Serapis werediscovered. The Milesian colony that preceded this city worshipped the chthonic god Derzelas and was called Odessos. Acampaign aimed at this city failed to receive expected aid from the Karamanids and saw an early defeat at Zlatitsa Pass. Thatcampaign against this city was prompted by the fall of Novo Brdo and a subsequent bull from Pope Eugene IV, and latersaw Cardinal Julian Cesarini receive an oath of campaign from Wladyslaw III despite concurrent negotiations for the Peaceof Szeged. This city is not Kosovo, but it does name a battle where Wladyslaw was killed by Janissaries in front of the tent ofMurad II, forcing John Hunyadi to signal retreat for his Polish and Hungarian troops in 1444. That battle ended the Crusadenamed for this city, which failed to oust the Ottomans from Europe. Name this Black Sea port which is theheadquarters for the navy of Bulgaria.

This alliance drafted a secret war plan called Seven Days to the River, which was not made public until 2005. The creation of this alliance led to fears that it would launch an attack through the Fulda Gap. The first supreme commander of this alliance personally led an attack called Operation Whirlwind, easily defeating forces led by Pal Maleter. In this alliance's early days, some of its leaders were trained at the Klement Gottwald Military Academy. Events leading to the formation of this alliance include the signing of the Paris Pacts and the adoption of the Hallstein Doctrine, which denied the legitimacy of one member of this alliance. This alliance was governed by a doctrine stating that military intervention would be used to prevent abandonment of socialism. Name this alliance created in 1955 as a rival to NATO.

This leader's horse was named Zuljanah. A general named Hurr, whose name translates as "free", defected to join this leader's side. This man's younger brother had his arms cut off after being caught attempting to bring water to an army commanded by this man. This man was marching towards the city of Kufa, where he had many supporters, when he fought the battle for which he is most famous. On the holiday of Arbaeen, also called Chelom, pilgrims visit this man's tomb and namesake shrine. The beating of drums and pounding one's chest are among the rituals performed on the 10th of Muharram or Day of Ashura to mourn this man's death in battle against the Umayyads. Name this son of Ali who was killed at the Battle of Karbala.

An attack on the Oureghla Line allowed this leader to successfully ally his nation with France. This man ended the "turno" system, in which his nation's political parties alternated terms in power, and established the Patriotic Union, or UP, as the sole political party. Two years before this man came to power, his nation suffered a military disaster at the Battle of Annual. Along with General Berenguer, his eventual successor, this man's government won a war against the forces of Abd el-Krim and gained control of the Rif. This man's government exiled critics such as Miguel de Unamuno and his rule was followed by the unstable Second Republic, during which his son founded the Falange. Name this dictator of Spain from 1923-1930.

A rule banning the drinking of alcohol on the Senate floor was allegedly inspired by a former governor of this state, Silas Wright. David B. Hill served three terms as governor of this state, beginning when his predecessor was elected President. Vice Presidents from this state include Levi P. Morton, who served under Benjamin Harrison. Gideon Granger led a splinter faction of conservative Whigs in this state called Silver-Grays, who opposed the machinations of boss Thurlow Weed. This state's representative James Tallmadge was a key figure in the Missouri Compromise, and in the late 19th century this state fell under the sway of Republican boss Thomas Platt. Democratic factions from this state include one which split into Softs and Hards, and one named for a type of cigarette lighter, the Loco Focos. Name this home state of the Hunkers, the Barnburners, and Martin Van Buren, whose capital is Albany.

In this election, the issue of the incumbent seeing women soon after his wife's death wasmagnified when a typo caused the Washington Post to claim he "spent the evening entering Mrs.Galt." Over four thousand women picketed this election's DNC convention in St. Louis by wearingyellow sashes to create a "golden lane." Allan Benson replaced Eugene Debs on the Socialist ticket inthis year. It was popularly claimed that the loser of this election lost it by a handshake, as heappeared to snub Hiram Johnson at a California event. The loser in this election had defeated WilliamRandolph Hearst to become governor of New York and had resigned from the Supreme Court to run. Thewinner used the slogan "He Kept Us Out of War." name this election which gave WoodrowWilson a second term.

This group traditionally claims to be descended from the semi-mythical Bappa Rawal, whofounded the Mewar Dynasty and cared for the mystic who gave this group their name. A warsometimes named for these people ended with the Treaty of Sugauli, which was signed reluctantly byBhimsen Thapa. This group was composed of people from the Magar, Gurung, Lumbu and Raiethnic groups. One group of these people has the motto "Better to die than live a coward" and hasmembers who carry a famous curved dagger called the kukri into battle. Actress Joanna Lumleywas at the forefront of a "justice campaign" to provide former members of that group with the right tosettle in Britain. Give the name for these Nepalese people famed for their service in theBritish Indian Army.

One story relates that this man lacked the respect of the people until he invited them to a banquetwhere he transformed stone into gold and water into wine. According to another story, he spiked aforest spring with wine to trick Faunus and Picus into revealing their secrets. This mancommissioned the Salii to guard the mysterious bronze shield which fell from the heavens during hisreign, and dismantled the group of armed guards called the Celeres. This man ascended to powerafter his predecessor dissappeared mysteriously in a storm. He instituted the position of Pontifex andcommissioned the Vestal Virgins, in addition to teaching the proper ways to worship this gods. For 10points, name this predecessor of Tullus Hostilius and successor of Romulus, the pious second king of theRomans.

One important case in which this status was found not to apply was Original Appalachian Artworksv. Topps Chewing Gum. Generally, disclaimers and acknowledgement do not enhance this status. Ithas been deemed an affirmative defense ever since 1994's Campbell v. Acuff-Rose, a case involving a 2 Live Crew song. As set out in section 107 of title 17 of the U.S. Code, the four factors that determinewhether this status applies are effect upon market value, the nature of the original source, whethercommercial value is being sought, and the amount used. Identify this status which can applywhen parodists, researchers, or others republish some amount of a copyrighted work.

After World War I, the Entente set the border between these two countries at the Foch line, whichcaused a conflict between them known as the Sejny Uprising. One of these countries sent Henry ofMasovia to negotiate the Ostrow Agreement with the other. Collaborationist forces in one of thesecountries massacred over fifty-thousand civilians in the Ponary massacre. The head of one of thesecountries instigated Zeligowski's Mutiny in the other. The combined forces of these two nationskilled Ulrich von Jungingen and defeated his Teutonic Knights at the 1410 Battle of Grunwald. Otherfriendly acts between these nations include the Union of Krewo and the Union of Lublin, which wasenacted by Sigusmund II Augustus. Name these countries that formed a commonwealthwhich had joint capitals at Warsaw and Vilnius.

In his work with Gustav Retzius, this man observed that the nerve fibers of the spinal cords ofhagfish lacked myelin sheaths. He designed a series of namesake passports that were issued tostateless refugees by the League of Nations. This man's other work as a diplomat includednegotiating the 1923 population exchange in which millions of Greeks and Turks switched countries.He prodded the British navy and directed the Red Cross in overseeing the repatriation of over400,000 Soviet prisoners of war, which earned him the Nobel Peace Prize. After submitting hisdoctoral thesis on zoology, this man became the first to cross the interior of Greenland. Aftertheorizing that a ship frozen in ice would drift towards the north pole, he commissioned the ship Fram forhis 1893 expedition. Name this brilliant Norwegian scientist, explorer and diplomat.

The first count of this region was Baldwin Iron Arm, who was granted this territory by Charles the Bald. The House of Dampier was the last independent dynasty of this region. This region was the starting point of the Beeldenstorm, a popular movement that saw the smashing of Catholic church decorations. During one incident in this region, those who could not pronounce the phrase "shield and friend" were massacred. A church in this region's city of Kortrijk was once decorated by hanging footwear that had been captured during the Battle of the Golden Spurs, in which this region defended its independence from France. This region was the site of the Spanish Fury, in which thousands of civilians were killed in the city of Antwerp. Name this region of Belgium that speaks Dutch.

The city of Cologne was briefly expelled from the Hanseatic League for accepting special trade privileges from this King of England, who fought a four year Anglo-Hanseatic War. This king signed the Treaty of Fotheringhay with the Duke of Albany, a pretender to the Scottish throne, as part of an attempt to overthrow James III of Scotland. This king signed the Treaty of Picquigny, under which he renounced English claims to the French throne in exchange for money from Louis XI. This king ended a brief period of English history called the "readeption". A conspiracy to overthrow this king was allegedly led by George, Duke of Clarence. After this king's death, the Titulus Regius invalidated his marriage to Elizabeth Woodville, causing him to be succeeded by his youngest brother, Richard. Name this first king from the House of York, the father of the Princes in the Tower and rival of Henry VI.

This city served as the first capital of the 5th century Burgundian Kingdom. This city was the siteof international conferences in 1927 and 1932 which failed to extend the naval limitations imposed bythe Washington and London conferences. Guillaume Farel was exiled and went to NeuchÃ¢tel afterstarting the Reformation in this city. The first meeting of Reagan and Gorbachev occurred here, andthe fall of Dien Bien Phu affected a conference in this city which divided Vietnam and failed to uniteKorea. Its citizen Henri Dunant was inspired by Battle of Solferino to hold a humanitarian conference inthis city. Name this Swiss city which is the namesake of a series of international conventionsgoverning military conduct.

This president signed the law abolishing DC's mandatory death penalty for first degree murder.He launched grand jury investigations and switched defense contracts after U.S. Steel violated a tacitagreement in raising their prices six percent, forcing the hike in prices to be rescinded within threedays. He stated his desire to "splinter the CIA into a thousand pieces and scatter it into the wind." Hespoke of a wish for "not merely peace in our time but peace for all time" in his commencementaddress at American University, in which he announced the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty. Hemobilized the Alabama National Guard to confront George Wallace in his stand in the schoolhouse door,and promised significant aid to Latin America as part of his Alliance for Progress program. He authorizedthe arming of exiles for the disastrous invasion of Cuba at the Bay of Pigs. Name thissuccessor to Dwight Eisenhower as President of the United States.

Oneida supporter John Humphrey Noyes was an early supporter of this movement, which helabeled stirpiculture. One of this movements greatest early champions was Charles Davenport, whoconvinced the railroad widow Mrs. E. H. Harriman to found the ERO. Victories for this movementincluded a 1924 Supreme Court case which upheld a Virginia law written by Harry Laughlin andwhich was partially overturned by Skinner v. Oklahoma. Institutions associated with this causeincluded a committee staffed by Alexander Graham Bell and Luther Burbank and the doctoredphotographs included in Henry Goddard's book about the The Kallikak Family. Cereal inventor JohnHarvey Kellogg also subscribed to this movement, which was supported in the case Buck v. Bell andassociated with "Better Baby" contests at State Fairs. It was based on the ideas of Sir Francis Galton andco-opted the work of Alfred Binet and Theodore Simon. Name this arm of scientific racismwhich sought to improve the genetic profile of the United States through forced sterilization and breedingrestrictions.

This man came to power by winning a succession war over Kutalmish, whose son established theindependent state of RÃ»m. In his early campaigns, he sacked the Cappadocian capital Kayseri beforemarching on Armenia and Georgia. According to Edward Gibbon, this man died when he waved hisbodyguards away and tried to shoot an assassin with his own bow. His adviser Nizam al-Mulk, whowrote The Book of Government and established a namesake system of Islamic higher education, alsoserved as vizier for his son Malik Shah I. This man's greatest victory occurred when the defection ofsome Cuman and Pecheneg mercenaries allowed him to capture Romanes IV Diogenes. Name this great Seljuk sultan who defeated the Byzantines at Manzikert.

After his forces lost the Battle of Renty to Francis, Duke of Guise, this ruler was forced to accedeto the demands of the secret Treaty of Chambord and cede the "Three Bishoprics" to France. He wastutored by future pope Adrian of Utrecht, who worked with Cardinal Jimenez as regent during thisman's minority. His aunt Margaret of Austria negotiated the Lady's Peace of Cambrai. Hisundisciplined and unpaid army kidnapped Pope Clement VII and sacked Rome during his waragainst the League of Cognac. He mimicked a triumph in his entry to Rome before challenging his rivalFrancis I to single combat. This man defeated Philip of Hesse and the other Lutherans of the SchmalkaldicLeague at Muhlberg, after condemning Luther at the Diet of Worms. Name this first king of aunited Spain who also ruled the Holy Roman Empire during the Reformation.

One member of this family was caught doping and kicked off the soccer team Perugia after onegame. Another member of this family had his book deal dropped after his thesis at the LondonSchool of Economics was revealed to have been plagiarized. Another of its members was arrested inGeneva in 2008 after being accused of assault by two servants, prompting a boycott of Swiss goodsand the expulsion of Swiss companies from his country. Another member of this family invented"Jamahiriya," and gave a February 2011 interview under a large white umbrella. Four members of thisfamily were killed in May 2011 airstrikes, and its patriarch wrote the Green Book and is protected by afemale bodyguard corp called the Amazonian Guard. Name this family whose patriarchMuammar is the leader of Libya.

This man's famous speeches include one in which he threatened to break the legs of any member of his party who did not join a boycott of the legislature, and one in which he said his nation would accomplish a certain goal "even if we have to eat grass." This man returned tens of thousands of POWs to his nation by signing the Simla Agreement. This man was the founder of a political party called the PPP, or People's Party. This man assumed power after his country had been destabilized by a separatist movement led by Sheikh Mujib. After being removed from power in the July 5 Coup, this man was put on trial for attempting to murder a political opponent named Ahmed Kasuri and was hanged, possibly on the orders of his successor Mohammad Zia. Name this prime minister of Pakistan during the 1970's, whose office was later held by his daughter Benazir.

This city was called Argentoratum by the Romans. In 1518, this city was home to one of the largest recorded outbreaks of "dancing mania", when over 400 people led by Frau Troffea spent a month dancing in the street, many dying of heart attacks or exhaustion. In 1609, John Carolus published the world's first newspaper, the Relation, in this city. The reformation in this city was led by Martin Bucer, who later moved to the court of Henry VIII of England. The medieval romance "Tristan" was written by a resident of this city named Gottfried. A bilingual treaty signed in this city is an important source for the early French and German languages and divided the territories of Charles the Bald and Louis the German. Apart from its namesake "oaths", this city is best known for its large Gothic cathedral, being home to the European Parliament, and for frequently switching between German and French control. Name this largest city in Alsace.

A Prince of Transylvania with this name controversially abdicated his throne to the Austrians in 1598, after being offered the title of Duke of Opole and land in Silesia. One king with this name lost the battle of Stangebro, leading to the slaughter of his supporters in the Linkoping Bloodbath and the accession of Charles IX. A Catholic king of this name is depicted holding an enormous cross on a namesake column in one European capital. The future King Henry III of France briefly served as King of Poland after the death of one Polish king of this name. One ruler of this name was defeated at the Battle of Nicopolis, ending his Balkan crusade against the Ottoman Empire. Kings of Poland with this name include one nicknamed "the old", one who tried to create a personal union with Sweden, and one who created the Union of Lublin, which strengthened ties with Lithuania and created an elected kingship. Give this name shared by the last Jagiellon king of Poland and a Holy Roman Emperor from Luxembourg.

This state's largest city was targeted by a federal corruption probe called "Operation Plunder Dome", which led to the conviction of long-time mayor Vincent "Buddy" Cianci. During the Civil War, a future governor of this state led the unsuccessful "mud march", ordered the arrest of Ohio copperhead Clement Vallandigham, and captured a namesake bridge at Antietam. Apart from Ambrose Burnside, this was the home state of Senator William Sprague, who became a powerful patron of Salmon P. Chase after marrying his daughter. This state was home to the Battle of Acot's Hill, an uprising by opponents of Governor Samuel Ward King, part of a larger conflict between the Charterites and the People's Convention. One founder of this state was an adherent of Antinomianism. Name this New England state home to Dorr's Rebellion and founded by Roger Williams.

One participant in this event protested that she was chairwoman of the Academy of Sciences afterbeing accused of having someone write scientific papers in her name. Another of its participantscontinually announced that he would only speak to the "Grand National Assembly." That mandenied owning a Swiss bank account, claimed he lived in a normal apartment instead of a palace, andsaid he had guaranteed every citizen two hundred kilograms of wheat. The subjects of this event hadbeen apprehended after flying by helicopter to Snagov, and were accused of genocide for ordering amassacre at Timisoara. This event lasted for a little over an hour on Christmas Day before its twosubjects were sentenced to death and shot. Name this 1989 trial during the RomanianRevolution.
trial of Nicolae and Elena Ceausescu

This civilization's religious practice included worship at open air temples called "peaksanctuaries," which were stocked with clay representations of humans and animals. The mostcommonly depicted goddess of these people was a bare breasted female holding a cat on her head anda snake in each hand. They also originated the worship of the goddess Britomartis, and frequentlyused the symbolic "horns of consecration" in their art. The existence of sites like Mallia, Gournia,and Zakros has led historians to divide their history into four "palatial" periods. A massivevolcanic eruption on Thera has been postulated as the cause of this civilization's decline in the 15thcentury BCE, when they were occupied by Myceneans and maintained only Knossos. Most knowledge ofthem comes from excavations by Arthur Evans. Name this early Linear A using Greekcivilization on Crete.

During the rule of this dynasty, the admiral Shi Lang won the Battle of Penghu to force thesurrender of the Kingdom of Tungning. That battle was part of a larger conflict in which its forcesdefeated leaders from Yunnan, Fujian, and Guandong in the Rebellion of the Three Feudatories andconquered the pretender Koxinga. This dynasty produced the two longest reigning emperors of China,one of whom attacked Vietnam and Burma in the Ten Great Campaigns. It was established after the ShunDynasty was set up by Li Zicheng. This dynasty of the Kangxi and Qianlong Emperors entered foreignwars after the appointment of Commissioner Lin Zexu and the Arrow Incident. Name thisdynasty which fought the Opium Wars with Britain and was led by Manchus.

The Spanish captured this city in a surprise 1596 attack, but returned it two years later in theTreaty of Vervins. The chief method of defending this city was a system of sluices which wereprotected by Fort Nieulay. By surprising the defenders of Nieulay, Francis Duke of Guise was able totake this city in 1558. After allowing this city to fall, Mary Tudor claimed its name written on herheart. Philippa of Hainault persuaded her husband to spare the lives of citizens of this city after aprotracted siege that followed the Battle of Crecy. Edward III spared this city in exchange for six ofits citizens walking out with nooses around their necks. Name this French city whichoverlooks the narrowest point of the English Channel, and whose Burghers were sculpted by AugusteRodin.

While serving under Frederick Funston during the occupation of Veracruz, this man wasrecommended for a Medal of Honor for his efforts in securing some locomotives. During World WarI he served as Chief of Staff of the Rainbow Division, which was composed of National Guardsmenfrom dozens of states. This man lengthened and modernized the course load among his other reformsas Superintendent of West Point. He retroactively received the first Purple Heart after reinstatingthe medal and calling for its redesign as Chief of Staff of the Army. He offered a dissenting voice on Billy Mitchell's court martial, and after World War II he served as commander of occupied Japan. Hewas replaced by Matthew Ridgway after criticizing Truman's Korea strategy. Name thisAmerican general who declared "I will return" as commander of U.S. Forces in the Far East during WorldWar II.

According to one story, this man earned his nickname by assaulting his tailor, and his career ended when he was arrested for robbing a bank messenger in Ohio. This man became the undisputed leader of his group after his partner Vincent Drucci was shot by the police. Earlier, Drucci and this man had been lieutenants of Hymie Weiss, who had been gunned down in front of Holy Name Cathedral. This man may have ordered the killing of "Machine Gun" McGurn in an act of revenge. This gangster's minions included "Gorilla Al" Weinshank and "Tight Lips" Gusenberg, and he was a protege of bootlegger Dion O'Banion. Seven of this man's followers were attacked by fake police officers in a garage during the Saint Valentine's Day Massacre. Name this Irish gangster from the north side of Chicago, the most notable rival of Al Capone.

France briefly participated in this war by launching a naval blockade, but withdrew under the Mackau-Arana treaty. Admiral Manuel Blanco was put on trial for treason for negotiating an unauthorized peace treaty during this war. Just prior to this war, the eventual losers sponsored an attempt by Ramon Freire to overthrow the government of the eventual winners. Diego Portales, the powerful defense minister who started this war, was assassinated in its second year, greatly increasing public support for this conflict on the winning side. The decisive battles of this war were the naval Battle of Casma and the Battle of Yungay on land. This war stopped the ambitions of General Andres de Santa Cruz and ended with the occupation of Lima. Name this 1836-39 war in which Chile and Argentina successfully prevented the merging of Bolivia and Peru into a single country.

Upon coming to power, this ruler exiled the unpopular German-born foreign minister, Adrey Osterman. This ruler signed the Treaty of Abo with Sweden, thereby gaining control of southern Karelia. This ruler's armies were ineptly led by Count Buturlin. This ruler was the supposed target of the Lopukhina Conspiracy, which was fabricated by French diplomats seeking to undermine this ruler's foreign minister, Count Bestuzhev. While allied with Austria, this ruler's forces won a great victory at the Battle of Kunersdorf, but were unable to follow up. This ruler came to power by overthrowing the infant Ivan VI and the regent Anna Leopoldovna. This ruler's death was called the "Miracle of the House of Brandenburg" by Frederick the Great, because her successor made peace with Prussia. Name this female empress who led Russia during the Seven Years War.

An inscription discovered in Gherla, Romania suggests that an army personally led by this man may have attempted to reach the source of the Danube, but most scholars think the inscription was carried there from Macedonia or Thrace. This man's wife was Princess Ardusnamuya and his only known son was named Artontes. This man's father, Gobryas, was one of the assassins of Gaumata. The maximum extent of this general's conquests are noted in his master's Davia Inscription. This man lost naval support when his fleet was wrecked at Mt. Athos. At his most notable engagement, this general made camp along the Aesopus River and attacked an army camping in the Kithaeron Mountains. According to Herodotus, this man's death turned the tide of battle in favor of his opponent, Pausanius. Name this general who led the Persian invasion of Greece and was killed at the Battle of Plataea.

A three part test for whether or not these entities apply was instituted by the 1955 Glenshaw Glasscase. The White court ruled that they did not violate the Due Process clause in the Brushaber case. InSpringer v. United States, the court ruled that one of these was indirect and not direct and thus didnot need to be apportioned among the states according to population. The Constitution states that theycan exist "without regard to any census or enumeration." Opposition to the Wilson-Gorman Tariff centeredaround its imposition of one of these entities, which was ruled unconstitutional by Pollock v. Farmers'Loan and Trust Company. Pollock was nullified and these were allowed by the Sixteenth Amendment. For10 points, name this type of tax.

One leader of these people was killed by the Gepid leader Ardaric at the Battle of Nedao. Theywere led by Uldin, who beheaded the Gothic leader Gainas and sent his head to Arcadius. Theirleader Rugila was struck by lightning during an invasion of Thrace. An empire formed by thesepeople collapsed after the succession of Ellac. One leader of these people won a large tribute from Theodosius after winning the Battle of the Utus and invading the Balkans. An oft-debated historicalmystery concerns what Pope Leo I offered these people to get them to turn back from Rome. One of theirleaders killed Theodoric I but lost to Flavius Aetius at the Battle of Chalons. Name this groupled by a man who killed his brother Bleda and was nicknamed the Scourge of God, Attila.

In the lead up to this battle, one side provided fodder for propaganda by allegedly massacringsixteen hundred people in the sack of Bolton. As this battle ended, a group of infantry "Whitecoats"held their ground against wave after wave of cavalry charge in a famous "last stand." The winningside at this battle consisted of three armies, including the Eastern Association under EdwardMontague, the Earl of Manchester. This battle resulted from an attempt to relieve the Marquess ofNewcastle at the Siege of York. At this battle, Covenanters under the Earl of Leven joined Parliamentariansunder Lord Fairfax to defeat Prince Rupert of the Rhine, forcing the royalists to abandon the north ofEngland. Name this 1644 battle, the largest engagement in the English Civil War.

These events were the subject of a 1997 play by Moises Kaufman. One theory holds that theywere prompted by the death of the Viscount Drumlanrig, which caused pressure to be put on PrimeMinister Rosebery. A.E. Housman was inspired by these events to write "he can curse the God thatmade him for the colour of his hair." The first of these sought to prove libel against the boxingaficionado Marquess of Queensberry. In the second of these events, their subject gave a famousresponse when asked to explain "the love that dare not speak its name." The third ended in the jailterm which prompted the writing of De Profundis and "The Ballad of Reading Gaol. Namethese events in which the author of The Importance of Being Ernest was accused of indecency.

This publication was losing money until its controversial coverage of a documentary film titled"The Birth of a Baby" got it banned in dozens of states and vastly increased its subscriptions. Itsstaffers accidentally destroyed or blurred most of Robert Capa's D-Day photographs. An editorialby this publication's editor coined the term "American Century." It also published NormanMailer's account of the Apollo 11 mission and Ernest Hemingway's Old Man and the Sea. Thisperiodical published Alfred Eisenstaedt's picture of a sailor kissing a nurse. Its first cover was aphotograph of Fort Peck Dam, and it also published Margaret Bourke-White's series about Gandhi. For 10points, name this prominent photojournalism magazine.

In this city, false newspaper reports alleging violence towards white women sparked thethree-day 1906 Race Riot. This city's Paschal's Restaurant was an unofficial headquarters of theCivil Rights movement. The Anti-Defamation League was founded after the lynching of this city'scitizen Leo Frank, which caused an exodus of half its Jewish population. Its longtime mayor WilliamHartsfield tried to market it as the "city too busy to hate" during the 1950s. Martin Luther King Sr.led the Ebenezer Baptist Church in this city. A 1964 Supreme Court case emerging from this city ruledthat congress did not exceed its powers under the Commerce Clause by prohibiting discrimination in amotel. Booker T. Washington's pragmatic approach in a speech given at an Exposition in this cityprompted Du Bois to call it a "compromise." name this capital city of Georgia.

This country's leader Dr. Arnulfo Arias had each of his three terms as president cut short bymilitary coups. It celebrates Martyrs' Day to commemorate the 1964 incident in which rulesforbidding the raising of its flag led to riots. A famous photograph shows a thug from this country's"Dignity Battalions" beating bloody Vice Presidential Candidate Billy Ford. After World War II,most of the power in this country was held by its National Guard, whose leader Omar Torrijossigned a 1977 treaty with Jimmy Carter. After Guillermo Endara's 1989 electoral victory was thrown out,this country was invaded in Operation Just Cause and its leader was forced to surrender after beingbombarded by loud music in the Vatican Embassy. Name this central-American country ledby Manuel Noriega which clashed with the United States over control of its "canal zone."

As an officer in the First Infantry Regiment, this man was said to hide in the bushes in order catchhis men drinking. He was killed when General Roger Hale Sheaffe detonated an ammunition store,sending a large rock at his head. This man signed a "Treaty of St. Peters" with the Sioux,accomplishing his namesake purchase in Minnesota. He died leading the amphibious assault on theBritish garrison at York during the War of 1812. He falsely claimed Leech Lake was the source of theMississippi, and some theorize that this man was intentionally captured and taken to Mexico byCommandant General Salcedo after General James Wilkinson sent him to explore the Great Plains. For 10points, name this explorer and namesake of a Colorado mountain.

Unrest broke out in this city after the Manzano brothers killed the Enruique brothers in a ballgame, prompting their mother Maria to hunt down and behead their killers. A popular legend heldthat a cave in this city under the Church of St. Cyprian hosted Satan as he taught heresies.Christopher Columbus had his request for an expedition denied by a hearing in this city. CalledHelmantica in Roman times, this city was the namesake of a school of thought pioneered by Francisco de Vitoria which adapted Aquinas's notion of "just price." Wellington was praised for defeating"40,000 Frenchmen in 40 minutes" at a Peninsular War battle here in which he finally defeated Marmont,allowing him to enter Madrid. Andreas Vesalius was tried for heresy in this city by an institution whichtrained St. John of the Cross, Luis Gongora, and Miguel de Cervantes. Name this home of theoldest university in Spain.

The Supreme Court cases of Norman v. Baltimore and Nortz and Perry v. U.S. Addressedcontractual clauses regarding this substance. That was in the wake of Executive Order 6102, whichcriminalized the possession of this substance in most circumstances. Throughout most of the 1960s,an attempt to stabilize the trade in this substance was made through the "London Pool." The 1971 "Nixon shock" was the unilateral American cessation of the sale of this substance for dollars, endingthe "exchange system" for it that prevailed under Bretton Woods. In contemporary times, companies suchas Liberty Dollars attempt to sell illicit currencies made from, what substance, which wasonce the reserve "standard" for American currency and which delights figures such as Francisco Pizarroand Ron Paul?

One leader of this navy invented "floating batteries" to sack Sfax and besieged the Barbarystronghold of Tunis aboard his flagship the Fama. Alexius I Comnenus allied with this navy to retakethe Balkans during the Norman invasion of the Byzantine Empire. This navy lost to Kemal Reis'sOttoman fleet at Zonchino, the first sea battle in which both sides used cannon. Its victories causedits leader to take a title meaning "Commander of three eighths of the Roman Empire." It convertedsome of its large merchant ships to create the first galleasses. One ship in this navy was called the "bucentaur" and was used in an Ascension Day ceremony in which a ring was thrown into the sea. Thisnavy formed the largest share of the allied forces at Lepanto, and cunningly redirected the Fourth Crusadeto Constantinople. Name this navy commanded by the Doge.

Juan Luis Vives's tract about the education of women is dedicated to and modeled after thiswoman. She withdrew from court life when she learned that her husband had impregnated ElizabethBlount, who would bear the bastard Duke of Richmond. She served as regent for one year while herhusband joined Maximilian I in defeating French forces at Guinegate. While regent, she sent thebloodied coat of James IV to her husband after the Earl of Surrey defeated a Scottish invasion at Flodden. Originally betrothed to Arthur, Prince of Wales in the Treaty of Medina del Campo, she wasdefended by Eustace Chapuys and Bishop John Fisher in the affair known as the "King's Great Matter."name Spanish princess whose marriage and annulment from Henry VIII prompted theEnglish reformation.

For much of its history, this city was surrounded by the Maratha Ditch, which was intended torepel Bargi invaders but was used to dump garbage. This city was traditionally founded by JobCharnock. The Treaty of Alinagar was signed after repairs to Fort William led to strife in this city.It was the site of a duel between Philip Francis and Warren Hastings, who had been impeached for escapingcorruption charges by having his accuser Nuncomar convicted of forgery. A general strike planned for thiscity on August 16 1946 resulted in thousands of deaths and rampant destruction on Direct Action Day.After taking this city from John Zephaniah Holwell in 1756, the Nawab Siraj-ud-Daula crammed over onehundred British prisoners into a tiny room. Name this Bengali city which was the site of a"black hole."

This organization was put out of commission for twelve hours in 1861 after John Wentworth firedeach of its employees. It was massively reformed by O.W. Wilson, who was appointed after several ofits employees were found to have formed a burgling ring in the Summerdale scandal. Thisorganization was forced to pay out almost two million dollars after killing Black Panthers MarkClark and Fred Hampton in a raid. George Ribicoff gave a speech saying that if George McGovernwere elected president, this organization would cease its "Gestapo tactics in the streets." Thatstatement occurred after it apprehended Pigasus the Immortal and battled with protesters for eightdays. August Spies was hanged after a pipe bomb thrown at members of this organization caused 1886riots. Name this organization involved in the 1968 DNC Convention and the HaymarketSquare massacre.

This battle began at Brawner's Farm with a Confederate attack on the 2nd Wisconsin, who engaged in a hot fire-fight with the Stonewall Brigade. Later in this battle, the 5th New York sustained the highest single-battle casualties of any infantry unit in the Civil War. This battle was preceded by the smaller battles at Thoroughfare Gap and Cedar Mountain. For refusing to make an attack at this battle, FitzJohn Porter was court-martialed, though his name was cleared after the war. The losing force at this battle was forced to retreat over the Stone Bridge, and this defeat led to the dissolution of the Army of Virginia. The losing commander at this battle, who had won fame for capturing Island Number 10 in the Mississippi theater, was reassigned to fight the Sioux in Minnesota. The winning commander followed up this battle by invading Maryland. Name this 1862 battle where Robert E. Lee defeated John Pope, fought near the site of the Civil War's first battle.

The oldest known document written by this man was a memorandum arguing that an archer militia should not be set up in Hangzhou, because the people there were weak, unskilled at war, and disloyal. This rival of Han Qi also opposed using the boajia system to draft soldiers, and instead unsuccessfully argued for the restoration of the fubing system that had been used by the Tang dynasty. This man resigned from serving the Shenzong emperor after the passage of the xin fa policies. This man is best known for writing the Zizhi Tongjian, a treatise on government whose title translates as "Comprehensive Mirror to Aid in Government", and for opposing price controls and the creation of pensions for the old and unemployed. Name this conservative scholar-official from the Song dynasty, the rival of Wang Anshi.

This city passed a law called the "Ordinances of Justice" which largely banned its ancient nobility from political participation. In this city, a leather bag called the borse was used to periodically choose the names of nine citizens at random: the first eight became part of the legislature, the ninth became this republic's chief executive. This city was home to the Spini family, who rose to prominence as bankers to Pope Martin V. Giovanni Villani was a chronicler of this city's history. It's not Venice, but this city was home to the monastery of San Marco. One family from this city adopted a coat of arms consisting of ten red balls, and one ruler of this city adopted a tax called la decima. This city was ruled by the Albizzi family following a 1378 revolt by carders of wool. Name this Tuscan city home to Savonarola and the Medici.

This man founded a school in the English village of Little Baddow after Archbishop Laud expelled him from a position at Chelmsford Cathedral. After fleeing prosecution for non-conformity by boarding the ship Griffin to America, he compiled his ecclesiastical views in the book A Survey of the Summe of Church-Discipline. This man was supported by Samuel Stone in a dispute with John Cotton. Thomas Welles and Roger Ludlow drafted a document inspired by this man's theories which was signed by the cities of Wethersfield and Windsor and which guaranteed universal manhood suffrage. This man's most famous action may have violated the Warwick Patent, a grant of land to the Earl of Warwick, and is commemorated by a plaque in the Cambridge Common marking the exact spot from which this man left Massachusetts to found Hartford. Name this founder of Connecticut.

While serving as Shadow Chancellor, this man defeated Reginald Maudling to become leader of his political party. During one election, this man's opponent nicknamed him "Selsdon Man", an attempt to portray his economic policies as primitive. This man's time in government is associated with a period of inflation called the "Barber Boom". As Prime Minister, this man re-introduced the halfpenny coin as part of his decimalization of currency. This man's government also adopted the Three Day Week, a form of electricity rationing, in response to a coal miner's strike, and he also led Britain into the European Community. This man resigned after calling an election that resulted in a hung Parliament. His single term as Prime Minister came between the two Labour governments of Harold Wilson. Name this leader of the British Conservative Party who preceded Margaret Thatcher.

This battle was fought at a stream called the Fontaone. A nearby village named Alessandria lends its name to a truce that was signed the day after this battle. The losing army at this battle was commanded by the Transylvanian nobleman Michael von Melas, who sent a fake spy to the opposing commander, allowing von Melas to open this battle with a surprise flanking attack. The decisive moments of this battle were a cavalry charge by General Francois Kellerman and the arrival, late in the day, of reinforcements under Marshal Desaix, who was killed in this battle. Along with the subsequent Battle of Hohenlinden, this battle helped end the War of the Second Coalition, led to the Treaty of Luneville, and strengthened the position of the newly-named First Consul. Name this June 1800 victory for Napoleon in northern Italy.

This practice creates a roundelle, which may have been used as a charm or talisman. This practice was performed after death in southern Siberia by the Tuvan people, and the use of this practice as a funerary rite may have spread with the Altaic and Turkish languages. The smaller "symbolic" variety of this practice was common in eastern Europe during the migrations period and was banned by King Stephen I of Hungary, suggesting that it was linked to pagan magic. This practice is strongly attested from Southern France during the neolithic, where a high survival rate is suggested by new bone growth, and it may have been performed to release evil spirits or relieve pressure. For 10 points name this oldest known surgery, consisting of drilling a hole in the human skull.

Haci I, a member of the Giray Dynasty, established one polity that was based around this sea and had its capital at Bakhchysarai [bak-chi-sarai]. Operation Bustard Hunt was part of one battle on the shores of this sea. In late medieval times, trade in this sea was dominated by the city of Caffa, which became a Genoese colony. Polities found on this sea include the Empire of Trebizond and one nation gained access to this sea by the Treaty of Kucuk-Kaynarca. One port on this sea has been besieged by such commanders as Gheorghe Avramescu, Erich von Mannstein, and Lord Raglan. This sea is connected to the Marmara by the Bosporus. Name this sea whose major ports include Sebastopol.

To mock this man's ambitions of social advancement, his political opponents accused him of bleeding himself to make his blood appear more blue. Early in his career, he led an agrarian political faction called the Amalgamators. As Chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, this man managed the impeachment of James Peck, a federal judge from Missouri, while as Chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee he attempted to block the Webster-Ashburton Treaty. In his highest office, this man turned down an offer from the King of Siam to send elephants to aid in American agriculture. This man named a treaty with Sir Richard Pakenham, which set the northern boundary of the United States at the 49th parallel. Along with J.Y. Mason and Pierre Soule, this man signed the Ostend Manifesto. Crises in this man's cabinet included the stormy resignation of Lewis Cass and attempts by War Secretary John Floyd to move entire arsenals of weapons to the south. Name this Pennsylvanian who was president at the start of the Civil War.

In 1975, a native of this country named Ariffin Mohammad declared himself the Mahdi and founded the Sky Kingdom movement, whose members are persecuted by this country's government. In the 1960's, this country won the Konfrontasi, an undeclared war with its southern neighbor. In 1969, the May 13 race riots broke out in this country, leading to this country's New Economic Policy. From 1981 to 2003, this country was governed by Mahathir Mohamad. This country's indigenous ethnic groups are called the "bumiputra" and enjoy special economic rights not granted to the richer minority ethnic Chinese. This country has territory on the island of Borneo, as well as the former British Strait Settlements. Name this southeast Asian country with capital Kuala Lumpur.

An unknown ruler of this country is depicted on a stone relief called the Madara Horseman. This country won the Battle of Acheloos against its southern neighbor. It was briefly ruled by the Cometopuli dynasty, but is more associated with the Dulo dynasty, founded by Kubrat, and the Asen dynasty, who built a capital at Great Tarnovo. One ruler of this country won the Battle of Pliska, while another earned his nickname by capturing Baldwin I at the Seventh Battle of Adrianople and defeating the Latin Empire. Apart from Kaloyan the Romanslayer, another ruler of this country, Samueli, is apocryphally said to have died of shock upon hearing that his army had been defeated and blinded by the Byzantine emperor. Name this Balkan country with capital Sofia.

Carsten Niebuhr first brought large copies of this writing system to Europe, and two important figures in the deciphering of this writing system were Irishman Edward Hincks and British army officer Henry Rawlinson. This writing system notably lacks a radix point and it contains only two symbols for numbers: one that stands for 1 and one that stands for 10, with a blank space being used for zero. One symbol in this writing system is transliterated as DINGIR and originally meant "god". Most symbols in this writing system represent a single syllable with one consonant and one vowel, though some can be logograms or determinatives. This writing system was designed for use with a stylus made of cut reeds, which were pressed into clay tablets. Name this writing system used in ancient Mesopotamia.

To signal the end of a radio blackout, one participant in this mission sent the radio message "please be informed that there is a Santa Claus." The decision by George Low to dramatically increase the scope of this mission, which was originally planned as a medium Earth orbit, may have been a response to the Soviet Zond 5 mission two months earlier. This mission was the last to be commanded by Frank Borman, who had earlier commanded Gemini 7. During this mission, astronaut William Anders took the photograph named "Earthrise", which was published in Life magazine and was later used by the environmental movement. The crew of this mission famously read the first ten verses of the Book of Genesis, which was broadcast to Earth on Christmas Eve. This was the first Apollo mission for James Lovell, who would later command Apollo 13, and the first to directly see the dark side of the moon. Name this first manned mission to orbit the moon.

During this conflict, a military unit named for King Deiotarus of the Galatians may have been annihilated; that unit was the 12th Legion. One leader in this conflict was accused of keeping a flaming piece of straw in his mouth, giving him the appearance of breathing fire. During this conflict, Julius Severus replaced Tineius Rufus as governor. Primary documents from this conflict were discovered in 1960 in the so-called "Cave of Letters". This conflict ended with the fall of the fortress of Betar. After this conflict, the city of Aelia Capitolina was built, along with the planned temple of Jupiter that sparked this conflict. The instigator of this conflict was supported by Rabbi Akiva, who proclaimed him the Messiah. Name this Jewish revolt against Hadrian, whose leader took the Hebrew name "son of a star".

Several newspapers biased in favor of this American political party were edited by Joseph Dennie, and the views of this party were championed by journalist William Cobbett. Journalists who opposed this party included James Callender and Benjamin Franklin Bache. This party once nominated Richard Stockton for Vice President. Members of this party wore dark ribbons in their hats, known as "black cockades". Later, this party's members were derisively called "blue-lights" for allegedly hanging lanterns along the coast to guide enemy ships. The Coodies were a faction of this party from Maryland. Theophilus Parsons led a Massachusetts political machine affiliated with this party. That machine, also associated with Timothy Pickering, was the Essex Junto. Notable for supporting the Alien and Sedition Acts, for 10 points name this political party of John Adams and Alexander Hamilton, the rivals of the Democratic-Republicans.

The first pope of this name minted the earliest known papal coins and was in power when King Desiderius of the Lombards threatened Rome, forcing that pope to invite Charlemagne's invasion of Italy. Another pope with this name had earlier sparked the Comuneros Rebellion when Charles V appointed him regent of Spain. Apart from the only Dutch pope, another pope with this name took the radical step of placing Rome under interdiction during Holy Week in order to weaken Arnold of Brescia and the Commune of Rome. That pope, a contemporary of Frederick Barbarossa, also issued the bull Laudabiliter which condemned the Synod of Kells held by the Celtic Church and authorized Henry II to invade Ireland. Give this papal name used by Nicholas Breakspear, the last English pope.

This empire was defeated at the Battle of Maule, which stopped its expansion south. This empire's society was organized around kinship groups called ayllu. The Wanka Confederation was an alliance of city-states against this empire. Residents of this empire could be drafted for 15 days to run messages between cities as part of the chasqui system. This empire adopted the agricultural practices of the earlier Wari culture and conquered the Chimu peoples. This empire was divided into four quarters, which converged on its capital city. Residents of this empire used quipu to communicate via knotted strings and an attempt to revive this empire was made at Vilcabamba. Name this empire that spoke Quechua and was based at Cusco.

After serving just one term, this man lost his seat in the House of Representatives to a candidate from the short-lived "Opposition Party". He also lost a Senate seat to a Whig named Henry Geyer, but his political career was long enough for his autobiography to be titled Thirty Years' View. This man led the successful effort to expunge the Senate's censure of Andrew Jackson. Despite being a slaveholder, he opposed the expansion of slavery at the end of his career. With the help of Vice President Millard Fillmore, this Senator blocked a plan to create a special committee to draft the Compromise of 1850, thus delaying that legislation and leading Mississippi Senator Henry S. Foote to draw a gun on this man. A failed bill introduced by this Senator was the basis for the Specie Circular, and this Democrat was the father-in-law of John C. Fremont. Name this long-serving Missouri Senator whose opposition to paper money earned him the nickname "Old Bullion".

On Fridays, holders of this office participated in a ceremony called "riding out", in which they traveled to a place of worship and accepted judicial appeals from citizens. Those in the presence of a holder of this office were required to perform proskynesis, or putting their forehead to the floor. Holders of this office were buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles. One holder of this office issued a law code called the "Ecloga". Another holder was nicknamed the "dung-named" for his campaign of forcibly marrying monks and nuns to expropriate monastic property; that man also convened the Council of Hieria. Yet another holder of this office divided his empire into themes. A notable holder of this office is the subject of the Anecdota, or Secret History, of Procopius and employed the generals Narses and Belisarius. Name this office, whose holder ruled the Eastern Empire based at Constantinople.

Walter Stennes was expelled from this group after leading two failed revolts demanding higher pay and better supplies. In its early years, this organization founded by Emil Maurice competed against a similar group called the Organisation Consul, or OC, which it later partially absorbed. Edmund Heines was serving as deputy leader of this group when he died. This group took its name from a military formation used in Hutier Tactics during the Spring Offensive. One member of this group wrote an anthem that began with the words "the Flag on High", and which would be renamed for him after his 1929 assassination. That man was Horst Wessel. Leaders of this group, including Ernst Rohm, were killed during the Night of the Long Knives. Name this first paramilitary wing of the Nazi Party, the predecessor of the SS.

This man was executed by the putative author of the Sisyphus fragment. A victorious general at the Battle of Cyzicus, he led the rescue of Alexicles and used it as a pretext to tear down the newly erected fortifications on Eetoneia. After the Battle of Arginusae, at which he served as a trierarch, he was prevented from saving drowning Athenian sailors by a storm. His defense at the ensuing trial was parodied by Aristophanes in The Frogs. One of the conspirators in the coup of 411 BC, he led the moderate faction of the Four Hundred in demanding the enfranchisement of all men of hoplite status. In 405 BC, he met King Agis II to negotiate the terms of the treaty that ended the Peloponnesian War. Famously dubbed "cothurnus" by Critias, name this Athenian statesman who was forced to drink hemlock for challenging the Thirty Tyrants.

Florida v. Mellon supplied a legal precedent for a tax-offset device in this law that avoided infringing on the constitutional powers of states. It was largely drafted by the Edwin Witte-directed CES, with support from Paul and Elizabeth Raushenbush, who had drafted similar legislation in Wisconsin. The NAACP supported Ernest Lundeen's alternative to this law, as Lundeen's plan did not exclude farm laborers and domestic workers. Its constitutionality was affirmed in a case whose majority opinion declared it was difficult to accept arguments that its application "is a use for any purpose narrower than the promotion of the general welfare," Steward Machine Company v. Davis. This law was criticized for not going far enough by supporters of Francis Townsend, creator of the Old-Age Revolving Pension Plan. Name this 1935 law that created national unemployment insurance and a a national benefits system for retirees.

Early in his career, this man lead the student organization F.U.C.I. While later tried to end a left-wing, right-wing split through the Civitas Humana organization. After leaving power, the UCIGOS special operations force executed Plan Zero in an effort to find this man, though the search was undermined by the DIGOS investigators failing to realize that an anonymous tip was referring to a street rather than a village. Inspector Leonardi was in charge of this man's protection, though his warnings about insufficiency of forces were ignored. Franco Moreno was the first to be arrested in connection to this man's eventual death, while later Mario Moretti was revealed to be the trigger man in this man's execution. Identify this Christian Democrat prime minister whose kidnapping by the Red Brigade represented the strife of Italy's Years of Lead.

This man pushed through a bill mandating that every health class in his state use the nutrition textbook he authored, OneHundred Years of Health. He engineered the election of Governor Ed Jackson, whose refusal to grant a pardon provoked thisman to release "little black boxes" detailing every public official under his thumb. This continual nuisance to Hiram Evansused the pseudonym "Mr. W.B.Morgan" to check into a hotel room with a woman who slipped by his bodyguard Shorty toswallow six bichloride of mercury tablets. This man tried to claim that Madge Oberholtzer had committed suicide, rather thansuccumbing to a staph infection from the chew marks this man leftft on her breasts. Name this Grand Dragon ofthe Indiana KKK, whose murder conviction led to the decline of the Klan nationwide.

This woman's popularity sffuered when her friend Pierre de BrÂ´ezÂ´e led a raid on the town of Sandwich on the pretense ofcoming to her aid. According to legend, she and her son were wandering lost through the woods when an outlaw gave hershelter in his cave. Another legend says she ordered a blacksmith to reverse the shoes on her horse so she could leave Mucklestonewithout being traced. She was the daughter of Rene I, the titled king of Naples. This queen was an ally of WilliamBeaufort, Duke of Somerset and William de la Pole, Earl of Suffolk. Though she was in Scotland at the time, she's been blamedfor ordering the execution of the Earl of Salisbury on the day after the Battle of WakeÂeld. She was exiled to France four yearsafter her husband was murdered in the Tower of London, and her son Edward died at the Battle of Tewkesbury. Name this queen who waged the Wars of the Roses for the Lancastrians, alongside her husband Henry VI.

One captain in this navy was the subject of Samuel Eliot Morison's Pulitzer Prize winning book subtitled "A Sailor's Biography."Barbara Tuchman's The First Salute takes its title from an encounter of this navy's ship, the Andrew Doria, with theisland of Saint Eustatius. One of this navy's fleffets was nearly eliminated by General Carleton and Thomas Pringle at the Battleof Valcour Island. Its disorganization allowed the escape of the outnumbered Glasgow in a nighttime engagement off BlockIsland. Its commander Esek Hopkins was relieved for unfairly splitting loot after its successful raid on Nassau. Its most famousofficer captured the HMS Serapis in the Battle of Flamborough Head after declaring "I have not yet begun to Âfight." For 10points, name this short-lived navy disbanded by 1785, which employed the Bonhomme Richard captain John Paul Jones.

A ruler of this polity besieged the city JaÂ´en three times, Ânally succeeding with the help of Paio Peres Correia. This polityagreed on its northern boundary with the treaty of Almizra. A law code from this state, the Fuero Juzgo, mainly consisted of atranslation of the Liber ludiciorum. One prince from this polity killed the son of GuzmÂ´an the Good while besieging the Castleof Tarifa during a rebellion against this polity's king Sancho the Brave. This polity fought with Portugal to win the Battle ofRÂ´ıo Salado against the Marinids. Henry of TrastÂ´amara took over this polity after the death of its ruler Peter the Cruel in itscivil war. One ruler of this polity, who wrote the songbook Cantigas de Santa Maria and introduced the Siete Partidas lawcode, was Alfonso the Wise. This state formed when Ferdinand III became ruler of both its namesake kingdom and LeÂ´on. For10 points, name this state whose queen Isabella married Ferdinand II of Aragon.

Before these events took place, a participant argued that the ZOMO's attitude caused some street disturbances near St.Brigid's Church. A letter written by one participant in these events noted that Church representatives like Cardinal Glempwould be present in the "miscellaneous" category and proposed a Council for National Understanding. During the last one ofthese events, the televised feed was paused behind a static image while music played for three hours aftfter the speaking order waschallenged by the leader of the Alliance of Trade Unions. These events took place after a massive wave of strikes, including oneat the July Manifesto coal mine in Upper Silesia. Culminating in an agreement which opened all Senate seats and thirty-Âfivepercent of the Sejm to free election, they resulted in a series of constitutional amendments called the April Novelization.One of those curtailed the power of Party Secretary General Jaruzelski. Identify these 1989 negotiationsbetween the coalition government faction and Solidarity in Communist Poland.

This ruler tapped Admiral Yahya Saleh to organize Hajjs for members of his family and began building a navy after conquering the port of Surat. As a child, this ruler was raised by his future father-in-law, Hindal Mirza. The finance minister Todar Mal created the dahsala tax system used by this ruler. This ruler dethroned Sultan Baz Bahadur during his invasion of Malwa. Upon first coming to power, this man was nearly overthrown by the invasion of King Hemu. This man attacked Sikander Shah to nullify the threat of the Suri Dynasty. He was forced to exile his childhood teacher, Bairam Khan, and fight his son and successor, Jahangir. Name this third Mughal Emperor, the son and successor of Humayun.

One battle in this war took place at the Pass of the Red Tower. Cassius Longinus was captured during this war, and committed suicide so that he could not be used as a negotiation tool. The attackers in the war began their offensive at the city of Egeta, located near a gorge called the Iron Gate. The possibly mythical Temple of Zalmoxis may have been destroyed in this war. After this war, the winning side used information from the traitor Bicilis to recover a treasure hidden by the losing commander in the Sergetia River. This war's climactic siege ended when the Romans found and destroyed the pipes leading into the enemy capital. Early in this war, the attackers built a massive stone bridge that was an early work of architect Apollodorus of Damascus. Name this war that ended with the Capture of Sarmizegetusa and the defeat of Decebalus, commemorated on Trajan's Column.

A member of this noble family who married Marie Clotilde of Sardinia as part of a peace deal was nicknamed "Plon-Plon," and a man of this house who renamed himself Franz got the Duchy of Reichstadt as a reward for quitting politics. One member of this royal house was wedded in Baltimore to Betsy Patterson, an Irish-American socialite, after which he was refused passage back to Europe until he abandoned her. It changed its crest from a gules-and-or design to an azure crest displaying a gold eagle with lightning bolts at its feet and adapted one symbol from the golden bee artifacts unearthed from the tomb of Childeric. The paramour of Countess Walewska and the husband of Eugenie de Montijo were in this family, which controlled Westphalia under King Jerome. Its most powerful member struggled against Pasquale Paoli, established the Batavian Republic, and installed his brother Joseph in Spain. Name this royal house of the First and Second French Empires.

It's not oil, but Hassai is the most promising source of this natural resource in Sudan, where Omar al-Bashir recently announced that his country had exported over $2 billion worth of this resource in 2012. An Australian named George Harrison is credited with helping another African nation become a major exporter of this resource, which was produced at Barberton and Pilgrim's Rest. The Soninke Wangara people obtained this resource from the Bambuk Mountains, and established a market for this resource at the city of Audaghost. The ability to produce this material at Bure led to the rise of the Soso Empire under Sumanguru Kante. The discovery of this resource in the Witwatersrand Basin led to the invasion of the Transvaal and the Boer War. Name this precious metal which in South Africa is turned into the Krugerrand coin.

In Gaul, this man put down revolts by the Cantabrians, built a complex network of roads, and built the Maison Carree in Nimes. This man repelled the Suebi to help out the Ubii, whom he resettled after founding a colonia on the west bank of the Rhine that became modern-day Cologne. This commander's victories at Mylae and Naulochus crushed the rebellion of "pirate king" Sextus Pompeius. As aedile, he expelled all astrologers from Rome before hiring engineers like Vitruvius to complete a massive project of urban renewal, whose success he proved by personally riding a boat through the Cloaca Maxima. As consul, he commissioned the initial construction of the Pantheon. This man benefitted from the defection of Quintus Dellius at a battle where he used Liburnians to outmaneuver his opponent's massive quinqueremes. Name this general under Augustus who defeated Marc Antony at the Battle of Actium.

One of this party's former leaders, Edith Cresson, caused the resignation of the entire European Commission when she was accused of hiring a dentist friend as an AIDS expert and other acts of fraud. This party traces its modern history to the Alfortville Congress, and it won an election on a platform called the "110 Propositions." Under Laurent Fabius, this party adopted moderate economic policies. In the 1990s, it adopted a strategy of "pluralism," seeking large majorities through coalitions, which resulted in this party finishing out of the top two in the 2002 elections. One leader of this party worked with Helmut Kohl to get the Treaty of Maastricht ratified and initiated a period of "cohabitation" by appointing Jacques Chirac as Prime Minister. Name this French political party that was once led by Francois Mitterand.

Early in his career, this man worked for the law firm of Erastus Culver. This man rejected an offer to become US Consul in Paris when asked to resign one office in favor of Edwin A. Merritt. This man appointed William Chandler as Secretary of the Navy and was the first head of state to recognize the Congo Free State. This man appointed Frederick Frelinghuysen as Secretary of State, replacing James G. Blaine. He signed a law named for the former running mate of George McClellan, which required exams and merit-based hiring to fight patronage. Name this signer of the Mongrel Tariff and the Pendleton Civil Service Act who became President on the death of James Garfield.

The central action of this event was an attempt to avoid a vote on the Fansher Amendement, and Leo Amery appealed for a resolution to this event. Part of this event involved a request to appoint Jacques Bureau to the Senate, despite having just resigned for accepting bribes. One figure involved in this event claimed that he said he would not perform a certain action until Arthur Meighen was "first given a chance to show whether or not he is able to govern," and the other namesake politician claimed it as a reason for independence even though he had been the one to request a resolution from London. Name this Canadian political crisis of the 1920s that broke out over the Governor-General's refusal to dissolve Parliament.

Following this event, people on the yacht Ouvea were arrested, but could not be detained. After this event, the married couple Sophie and Alain Turenge was detained and Charles Hernu resigned. Guilt for this event was eventually admitted by Laurent Fabius. As a result of this event, Fernando Pereira died. This event was planned to prevent interference at the Moruroa nuclear tests. In this event, Christine Cabon planted two mines that would detonate with some delay between them so that the first mine would provide a warning. It occurred in Auckland, New Zealand and was supposedly authorized by Francois Mitterand. Name this event in which a Greenpeace ship was sunk by agents of the French government.

During an election year, this publication published an editorial backing a candidate which was purported to be written by Stalin. The appointment of a poet to a chair position at a prominent University led to this publication printing the headline "Would You Let This Man Near Your Daughter?" This newspaper lost a large number of readers in a major city after a report that alleged soccer fans urinating on police and stealing from the dead. That headline was referring to the Hillsborough stadium disaster where Liverpool fans were blamed for interfering with a rescue effort, allegations which were later proved false. This publication printed the headline "Gotcha!" which was seen by many critics as celebrating the deaths of hundreds of enemy soldiers on the General Belgrano during the Falkland Islands War. Name this trashy British newspaper owned by Rupert Murdoch, the most widely read newspaper in the United Kingdom.

Prior to this engagement, one commander gave a speech in which he compared the inevitability of death to the marks left behind by a necklace. The losing side at this battle had been waiting for reinforcements from Al-Kufah, and that side consisted of only 72 soldiers at the beginning of the battle. The victor at this battle was betrayed by Hurr, who cursed the Kufans for blocking access to the river Euphrates. Prior to this battle, the governor of Al-Basrah was sent by Yazid I to warn tribal leaders of reprisal if they fail to keep order among their people. It is reenacted with the performance of ta'ziyyah and is commemorated on the 10th of Muharram. Name this battle where Hussein ibn Ali was killed, leading to the split between Sunni and Shiite Muslims.

The surrender of Hegra Fortress marked the end of organized resistance to this action, defenses against which were further weakened by Operation Alphabet. Oscarsborg Fortress provided the first counter-action during this event when it sunk the Blucher. The Shetlands Bus program helped those who either wanted to escape this action or aid its opposition. This event was precipitated by the Cossack's liberation of prisoners aboard the Altamark, which had sailed into waters that were later the site of the Battles of Narvik during this event. This event inspired the formation of Milorg and similar groups, one of which attacked hydroelectric plant in order to disrupt heavy water production. This event, which was immediately preceded by a similar action against Denmark, caused the flight of Haakon VII and opened the door for Vidkun Quisling's coup. Name this military campaign that began with the Kriegsmarine sailing up some fjords.

The song "And After the Farewell", which had been a Eurovision entry earlier that month, was played to signal the beginning of this event. The main actors of this event were junior officers disgruntled by the move to make conscript time count towards seniority. Admiral Americo Tomas fled the country during this event, which led to the accession of a seven-man military junta. The man who was the target of this event expressed his concern that power would "fall into the street", and refused to surrender to anyone below the rank of General. He ended up surrendering to General Spinola. This event was organized by the Armed Forces Movement, or MFA, and is sometimes called the 25th of April Movement. Name this military coup against Marcelo Caetano, named for the red flower its supporters wore, which led to the end of the Estado Novo in Portugal.

One ruler of this polity initiated Literati Purges that brought about the rise of the Sarim faction. In another incident in this polity, the execution of Bishop Berneux led to an outburst of violence against Catholic residents of this dynasty. One treaty forced on this dynasty led to the occupation of this dynasty's Port Hamilton. The founder of this dynasty was a general who was ordered to invade China, but instead led a coup. This dynasty was destabilized by succession crises called the Strifes of the Princes. During this dynasty's decline, its female ruler Queen Min was assassinated by foreign agents, and this dynasty was forced to sign the Treaty of Gangwha. This dynasty was destabilized by the Donghak Peasant Rebellion, which led to a successful Japanese invasion. Name this final Korean dynasty.

Frank Geyer, a member of this organization, discovered the bodies of the three murdered Pitezel children, and thereby helped capture H.H. Holmes. One member of this organization used the pseudonym "James McKenna"; that man, James McParland, captured Harry Orchard, who had assassinated the governor of Idaho, and successfully infiltrated the Molly Maguires. The founder of this organization gained fame after he foiled an assassination attempt on Abraham Lincoln, and this organization famously was hired by Henry Clay Frick to fight union workers during the Homestead Strike. Name this most notable American private security agency of the 19th century.

Prior to this conflict, representatives from both of the main sides debated in the Colloquy of Montreal. After this conflict's siege of Bram, 100 prisoners had their noses chopped off and were sent to Cabaret, a castle that formed a defense complex with the adjacent commune of Lastours. Peter II of Aragon met his end in this conflict's Battle of Muret, and the entire population of Beziers was supposedly massacred in this conflict. This conflict was sparked by the murder of Pierre de Castelnau, a papal legate of Innocent III. Notable moments in this conflict include the order "kill them all, because God will know his own" and the excommunication of Raymond VI of Toulouse. Identify this war in Languedoc that sought to wipe out a certain religious group of southern France.

This man created a large neon sign declaring "Peace, Work and Well-being," and his regime played back the screams of Martin Almada to his wife from his torture, causing her death. The Febrerista Party opposed this man, but was legalized after being deemed to no longer pose a threat. Martin Almada would later discover the so-called "Archives of Terror" documenting the crimes of this man who was supported by peasant irregulars known as the "barefoot ones." He lost power after being ousted in a coup lead by Andres Rodriguez, and himself took power following a coup against Federico Chavez. In one incident, after a failed coup attempt he was driven to the Brazilian embassy in the trunk of a car, which gave him the nickname "Colonel Trunk." identify this man responsible for the construction of the Yacyreta and Itaipu dams, the leader of the Colorado Party who from 1954 to 1989 led Paraguay.

Along with Randolph Churchill, Henry Drummond-Wolff, and John Gorst, this politician made up the Fourth Party, an offshoot of the Conservatives. Following his resignation from his highest post, this man's successor survived the Relugas Compact, which attempted to remove him from the leadership of the Liberal Party. This man's appointment to the post of Chief Secretary for Ireland may be the origin of the British phrase "Bob's your uncle," since his uncle was Robert Cecil, Lord Salisbury, who he later succeeded as Prime Minister. His enforcement of the Crimes Act in Ireland led him to be nicknamed "Bloody," and his government signed the Entente Cordiale with France. As Foreign Secretary under David Lloyd George, this politician sent a document later incorporated into the Treaty of Sevres to Walter Rothschild. That letter expressed the government's support for a Jewish homeland in Palestine. Name this British statesman who issued a famous "Declaration" in 1917.

This group's founder proposed a namesake "non-interest bond bill" in his magazine, The Cause and the Cure. A radical California politician named Carl Browne served as this group's second-in-command, and this group's founder named his son Legal Tender and later founded a newspaper called "Sound Money". This group called itself the "Commonwealth of Christ". It demanded the establishment of a 500 million dollar "Good Roads" program as part of its so-called "petition in boots". Founded in Massillon, Ohio, this group protested the government's inaction during the Panic of 1893. This group's most famous effort came to a halt when its leader was arrested for trespassing on the Capitol lawn. Identify this group of unemployed workers who marched from Massillon, Ohio to Washington.

Inexperienced members of this dynasty were aided by the "Book of Government." Forces of this dynasty put down Baba Ishak's movement with the help of Frankish mercenaries. This dynasty's founder defeated Al-Malik Al-Rahim, the last ruler of the Buyid dynasty. This dynasty's generals Chagri and Tughrul defeated the Ghaznavids at the Battle of Dandanaqan.The vizier Nizam al Mulk served members of this dynasty, and al Mulk's death at the hands of the Assassins may have been ordered by this dynasty's sultan Malik Shah I. A governor appointed by this dynasty, Zengi, created his own dynasty by reconquering lands from crusaders, and during the First Crusade this empire lost Nicaea and Antioch. Its most famous military success came when Romanus IV Diogenes was captured by Alp Arslan at Manzikert. Name this dynasty founded in 1037 in Anatolia.
